analytic.title: Verification of schedulability of real-time systems with extended time Petri nets Yasukichi 0 kawa

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.head: Most verification algorithms for schedulability of real-time systems are based on an approximate computation which only considers worst cases. Although they always find correct schedulings, in which any task never violates its deadline, those schedulings are sometimes too strict. In this paper, in order to verify schedulability more precisely we propose a verification method based on the state space traversal of the time Petri net that models the given real-time system and the given scheduling. W e also extend time Petri nets in order to model round-robin scheduling easily. Some experimental results obtained by the proposed method are shown.
Introduction
div.p: For hard real-time systems, schedulability analysis to verify that every task meets its deadline is the most critical process. This goal was achieved by rather adhoc manner for a long time. Recently, it has been tried by many researchers to analyze the schedulability more formally. Those works have made real-time systems more predictable [l]. Most algorithms, however, compute schedulings with the worst case analysis using given periodicity, computation time, and so on of each task. Thus, the obtained schedulings are correct, that is, any task never violates its deadline, but are sometimes too strict. If the additional information, for example, the structure of tasks, is given, then more precise analysis of the schedulability will be possible.

In this paper, we aim at developing a tool for the precise schedulability analysis. We model each task of real-time systems by time Petri nets. Petri nets are well-known to be useful in analyzing concurrent dynamic systems. Time Petri nets are obtained from Petri nets by associating each transition of Petri nets with two times representing real-time constraints. Thus, time Petri nets simply model dynamic and concurrent real-time tasks. The schedulability analysis is based on the state space traversal of the time Petri net modeling the given real-time system. Although 0-8186-7099-1/95 $4.00 Q 1995 IEEE the cost of this process is rather expensive, the analysis examining all firable transition sequences gives the precise results.

In [2], the author considers so-called slowdown caused by more than one tasks running simultaneously at one processor in round-robin manner. This phenomenon, however, can not be modeled easily by the original time Petri nets. Thus, in this paper, we propose one extension of time Petri nets which can simply model slowdown of tasks.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines real-time systems that we consider in this paper. In section 3, how to model such real-time systems by time Petri nets is described. The extended time Petri nets are also defined in this section. Section 4 presents how t o construct and traverse the state graphs of the extended time Petri nets. Some experimental results are shown in section 5. Finally, we summarize our discussion.

div.head: Real-time systems
div.p: We define real-time systems as in [2]. A real-time system consists of a set of tasks which share a processorl , a set of devices, and a set of resources. Each task i has its deadline Gi. For simplicity, a periodic task has the same fixed time interval between consecutive restarts as its deadline (i.e. task i will be restarted at every Gi). We call the set of pairs ( i , G i ) scheduling. Now, the schedulability verification problem for the given real-time system and the scheduling is to check if for every i, task i always meets its deadline Gi .

div.head: Tasks of real-time systems
div.p: We assume that each task in a real-time system has the following characteristics.

A task consists of a series of segments which are run in order. A segment may require resources. Such a segment is called a resource segment. If a segment Although multiple processor systems can be handled in our tool, we discuss uniprocessor systems in this paper for simplicity.

does not require any resources, then it is called a nonresoume segment. Resources are introduced to realize critical sections to use exclusively data areas, devices, and so on. A resource is allocated to one resource segment which requires the resource when the segment is started, and the resource is released from the segment at the end of its execution. The same resource is never allocated to more than one segments simultaneously.

A segment consists of processor operations and device operations. During a device operation, the segment uses a device instead of a processor. The same device can not be used by more than one segments at the same time. The time needed for a processor operation in a segment is given by the form [a, b], where a and b are constants. A processor operation with [a, b] continues its execution at least until the total allocation time of the processor t o this operation becomes a, and completes the execution before the total allocation time exceeds b. This expressibility of the deviation in processor times makes it easy t o model practical systems. Similarly, the operation time of each device in a segment is given by the form [a, b].

Figure 1 picked up from [2] shows an example of a real-time system with two tasks. The sections separated by bold vertical lines represent segments. "[1,2]" and so on represent the processor operation times or the device operation times. "Rl" is a name of a resource, and the sections with resource names are resource sections. The hatched horizontal lines represent processor operations which require resources.

When several non-resource segments are ready, those segments can run in round-robin manner if desired. In this case, those segments use a processor in specified running rates, and take more elapsed time than their given processor operation times2. This is called slowdown. Figure 2 shows an example of task execution in the real-time system of Figure 1 when GI = 3G2. As shown in the figure, task 1 is blocked four times ("block-a,b,c,d"), and the slowdown of both tasks occurs once. "block-a" and "block-d" are caused because the resource segment of task 2 obtains R1 earlier. Task 1 is blocked at "block-b" due to the busy device D1.

At "block-c", task 1 is preempted by the resource segment of task 2. The slowdown occurs when two nonresource segments run simultaneously. Under the above rules, [2] proposes a method to compute a scheduling in which every task meets its deadline. Since it is based on the worst case analysis, such Gi's are too strict in many cases.
In this paper, we add the following assumptions for simplicity :
1. Requests to devices or resources are handled by ring arbiters.
2. Resource segments that need more than one resources obtain all those resources at the beginning of the segments. Figure 1: An real-time system with two tasks.

div.head: Rules of task execution
div.p: Periodic task i is restarted at every Gi. While a resource segment runs, any other resource segments that need the same resource or any non-resource segments can not be started at least until the resource segment ends. Further, running non-resource segment can be preempted when a resource segment becomes ready, because resource segments have higher priority than non-resource segments. If a segment needs a device which is already being used by the other segment, the former segment has to wait until the device is released. When a ready segment has to wait (or be preempted) Other strategies using priority driven scheduling policies or handling requests by means of FIFO queues may be allowed in our model as long as they are expressed as finite state machines. However, those complicated strategies often require awful cost for the analysis.

The advantages of using time Petri nets to model real-time systems are : (1) concurrency can be modelled easily, (2) timing constraints with variation of Modeling with time Petri nets *Note that the processor operation times are defined in terms of the total allocation time for the processor.

processor/device operation times can be expressed naturally. Since the most critical case may occur when some processor/device operation times take less values than their maximums, considering the variation of operation times gives more precise solution for our verification problem. [Rl] is the property called one-safeness, and it simplifies the state enumeration algorithm.

div.head: Time Petri net models of tasks
div.p: Figure 3 shows an time Petri net model of a periodic task i. It consists of a timer part and a task body.
Aperiodic tasks are also modeled very similarly.
The timer part has two transitions and four places.

At every G,, the transition Ttimer2, which plays the role of a timer, produces two tokens. The token in Pinit activates the task body. In other words, the task body starts by consuming the token in Pinit. The token in Pstart together with the token in Pfin restarts the timer by producing a token in €'timer. When the task body completes its execution, it will produce a token in Pfin. If Pfin always gets a token earlier than the next firing of TtimerS, that is, a marking with Pstart = l , P f i n = 0 is not reachable, then it means that task i meets its deadline. Thus, the schedulability problem of task i is reduced to the reachability problem of time Petri nets.

The task body consists of non-resource segments, resource segments, and device operations. Since resource segments and device operations consume exactly the same times as their given processor/device operation times, its execution is naturally modeled by a single transition which has the minimal (maximal) operation time as the earliest (latest) firing time as shown in Figure 4. In order to realize exclusive execution of resource segments or device operation, time Petri net models of ring arbiters are placed before those transitions representing the processor/device operations. If it is guaranteed that only one non-resource segment runs at the same time and it is never blocked by resource segments, then the processor operation in such a non-resource segment is also modeled by a single transition like resource segments and device operations. However, if the slowdown occurs, completing the execution of those segments will take more time than the given processor operation times depending on their running rates. The blocking by resource segments like "block-c" in Figure 2 causes the similar effects. These phenomena require to change the earliest/latest firing times dynamically, which is not allowed in the original time Petri nets. Therefore, we propose here one extension of time Petri nets by which the various segment execution including slowdown and blocking is easily modeled.

div.head: Experimental results
div.p: We have implemented the proposed algorithm on a 135 MIPS UNIX workstation in C++. In this section, with this tool verifying the example shown in Figure 1, which we take from [2], is demonstrated. This realtime system has two tasks. Both of them are periodic, and their deadlines (equal t o their periodicity) are G1 and GZ. For simplicity, we fix the ratio of G1 and GI such that GI = 2G2 = 2k. Table 1 shows the results of verification for various k's. The initial value (37.0) of k is chosen from the result (GI = 74.728, G2 = 37.364) of [2]. In the table, "OK" means that the markings which violate the deadlines are never reached, that is, every task always meets its deadline. Roughly speaking, it is found from these results that optimal k exists between 30.4 and 30.5. If we choose 30.5, then it may not be optimal, but its error is at most 0.1. "time" shows the total CPU times for verification. More than 30% of them is used to solve the linear programing.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, in order to precisely verify the schedulability of real-time systems, we have proposed to model real-time systems with extended time Petri nets. We have also proposed the state space traversal algorithm for extended time Petri nets and implemented it. The extended time Petri nets naturally model even tasks running in the round-robin manner. The results obtained from the example show that the several schedulings which are considered to be wrong in [2] are correct. On the other hand, handling inequalities in the algorithm costs much time. We may suffer from the state explosion problem for medium or large real-time systems. We are now trying to obtain more efficient algorithm based on the proposed approach.
